subcommands.name: status
subcommands.description:
🗺️ Show a status

A single screen answering "what is running right now, and is it healthy":
the example currently running and its documentation link, the state of
every container (flagging the exited or restarting ones), the version of
every connector, the status and configuration of each of them, the topics
that exist, and whether an EC2 instance of yours is still up.

Everything comes from the running containers and from playground.ini, so
it is also the quickest way to get back your bearings after a break.

subcommands.name: doctor
subcommands.description:
🩺 Check that the container engine is ready for the playground

Reports which engine the 'docker' CLI is really talking to — 🐳 Docker or
🦭 Podman — and checks what has to be right before any example can start:
the engine is reachable, compose v2 is there, there is enough memory, and,
with podman, that short image names resolve, that privileged ports can be
published and that bind mounts will be readable from the host.

This is the one command that still runs when the engine is down, so it is
what to run first when an example fails before a single container starts.

Exits 1 if it found a blocking problem, 0 otherwise.

👉 Check documentation https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/how-to-use?id=%f0%9f%a6%ad-using-podman-instead-of-docker

subcommands.name: cleanup-ccloud-resources-after-run
subcommands.description:
🧹 delete the Confluent Cloud resources left by the last ccloud example

Connectors and topics created by a ccloud 'playground run' are recorded
with the run. On 'playground stop', and at the start of the next
'playground run', the ones still alive are listed and deleted:

  ask     list them and ask for confirmation (default)
  true    delete them without asking
  false   never delete them

Fully managed connectors are billed while they exist, and an
interrupted example never reaches its final 'playground connector
delete'. Resources of older runs, or created outside a run, are left
alone: use 'playground cleanup-cloud-resources --resource ccloud'.

subcommands.name: secrets
subcommands.description:
🔐 Credentials required by examples

Examples declare the environment variables they need. Store them once here
and 'playground run' loads them automatically, picking only the ones the
example at hand declares:

  playground secrets set SALESFORCE_PASSWORD    🔐 store it, prompted
  playground secrets check -f <example>         ✅ what is still missing
  playground run -f <example>                   🚀 loaded for you

📂 Where it is stored

In ~/.config/kafka-docker-playground, never in the repository, so it
survives 'git clean -fdx' and can never be committed by mistake:

  secrets.ini  0600  credentials, as a reference to the backend ('op://...', 'keychain:...'), not as a value
  env.ini      0644  plain variables, in clear text

A name containing PASSWORD, PASSPHRASE, SECRET, TOKEN, KEY, CREDS, PWD or
LICENSE is treated as a credential, anything else as a plain variable
(GCP_PROJECT, AWS_REGION, an account name, a URL). Use --secret or
--plain with 'playground secrets set' to decide yourself.

🏦 Backends

Where the credential values themselves are kept:

  - keychain     macOS Keychain
  - secret-tool  freedesktop secret service (GNOME Keyring, KWallet)
  - pass         the standard unix password manager
  - op           1Password, through the 'op' CLI
  - vault        HashiCorp Vault
  - file         clear text in secrets.ini, no encryption, last resort

With no configuration, the first available of keychain (macOS), then
secret-tool, then pass is used, and file is the fallback. op and vault
are never picked automatically, so that an example never blocks on an
unlock prompt. Choose one explicitly with:

  playground secrets backend op

op creates and rotates the items it stores. vault is reference-only:
create the secret in Vault, then point a variable at it. Any backend can
also reuse a secret you already have, instead of storing a new one:

  playground secrets link SALESFORCE_PASSWORD op://Private/sfdc/password

🗂️ Profiles

A profile is an independent set of variables, typically one per customer
or per support case, so last week's credentials never leak into this
week's reproduction model:

  - playground secrets profile customer-123456    🗂️ switch to it
  - playground secrets profile                    📋 list them, with counts
  - playground secrets list --profile default     🎯 use one just this once

Lookup falls back to the 'default' profile, so what is shared between all
of them (CONFLUENT_LICENSE, NGROK_AUTH_TOKEN) is stored there once.

🔍 Resolution order

  1. an exported environment variable, which always wins
  2. the active profile
  3. the default profile

So 'export FOO=bar' and 'source secret.properties' keep working, and
'playground secrets list' flags what the environment overrides.

⚙️ Configuration

  - playground config set secrets.backend <backend>      🏦 see above
  - playground config set secrets.profile <name>         🗂️ active profile
  - playground config set secrets.op-vault <vault>       🔑 1Password vault

PLAYGROUND_SECRETS_DIR, PLAYGROUND_SECRETS_BACKEND,
PLAYGROUND_SECRETS_PROFILE and PLAYGROUND_OP_VAULT override them for a
single command.

🍪 Deep dive: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/deep-dive-secrets

subcommands.name: set
subcommands.description:
🔐 Store a credential

Without --value the value is prompted without echo, so it never lands in
the shell history.

A name that looks like a credential (PASSWORD, SECRET, TOKEN, KEY, CREDS,
PWD, PASSPHRASE, LICENSE) goes to the secure backend, anything else is
kept as a plain variable. Use --secret or --plain to decide yourself.

Run again on a name already stored to rotate it. The value is then
updated where the existing reference points, which is not necessarily
the backend currently configured.

🎓 Tip: set the config key secrets.github-repo and every value stored
here is also pushed to that repository's GitHub Actions secrets
(not when PLAYGROUND_SECRETS_DIR points at another store).

options.description:
🔓 Value to store

❗ it will be visible in your shell history, prefer the prompt ❗

🔐 Treat the value as a credential, whatever the variable name is

It goes to the secure backend (keychain, 1Password, pass…) instead of
being kept in clear text.

Conflicts with: --plain

📝 Treat the value as a non sensitive variable

It is kept in clear text in env.ini, which is handy for a URL, an
account name or a project id.

Conflicts with: --secret
🗂️ Secrets profile to use (default is the active one)

subcommands.name: get
subcommands.description:
🔍 Show a stored credential (masked unless --reveal is used)

Resolved the same way an example does: an exported environment variable
first, then the active profile, then the default one.

options.description:
👀 Print the value in clear text

❗ it will be visible in your terminal scrollback ❗
🗂️ Secrets profile to use (default is the active one)

subcommands.name: unset
subcommands.description:
🗑️ Remove a stored credential

The value goes too, not only the reference: the keychain entry is
deleted, the 1Password item is archived.

A secret pointed at with 'playground secrets link' is left untouched,
since it belongs to you and not to the playground.

options.description: 🗂️ Secrets profile to use (default is the active one)

subcommands.name: list
subcommands.description:
📋 List stored credentials

Values are never printed: secrets are shown as a masked fingerprint
(last 4 characters and a sha256 prefix), which is enough to tell whether
it is the token you rotated yesterday. Plain variables are shown as is.

Two markers to look out for:

  ⚠️ overridden by the environment   an exported variable is what the
                                    example will actually get
  ❌ cannot be resolved              the reference is there but the
                                    backend gave nothing back, usually
                                    a locked session or a deleted item

options.description: 🔗 Show the backend reference instead of the fingerprint
🗂️ Secrets profile to use (default is the active one)

subcommands.name: link
subcommands.description:
🔗 Point a variable at a secret manager, without storing any value

The store then only contains a reference, which is safe to back up, sync
between machines, or share with your team.

Use it to reuse a secret that already exists, rather than storing a
second copy of it, and for the vault backend which playground never
writes to. The reference is resolved right away, so a typo or a locked
session is reported on the spot.

'playground secrets unset' drops the reference but leaves the secret
itself alone.

options.description: 🗂️ Secrets profile to use (default is the active one)

subcommands.name: check
subcommands.description:
✅ Show what an example needs, and what is missing

One line per variable, saying where the value comes from (environment,
or which backend and which reference) or how to store it. AWS and GCP
examples also get their ~/.aws/credentials and keyfile.json checked.

The list comes from the example itself: every variable it declares with
the standard 'Export it as environment variable or pass it as argument'
error string, which is also what 'playground run' loads.

Exits 1 when something is missing.

🎓 Tip: run it before a long example, it fails in a second instead of
several minutes into the environment startup.

options.description: 📄 Example script (default is the last example ran)
🗂️ Secrets profile to use (default is the active one)

subcommands.name: env
subcommands.description:
🐚 Export what an example needs into the current shell

This is the replacement for 'source secret.properties'. Instead of putting
every credential into every shell, it exports only the variables the example
at hand declares, read from the secrets store:

  source <(playground secrets env)

Handy when copy pasting pieces of an example script into a terminal. With no
--file it uses the last example ran, like 'playground secrets check'.

The shell code goes to stdout and everything else to stderr, so nothing
unexpected ever gets executed. Running it straight in a terminal is
refused rather than printing every value on screen, use --force for
that.

🎓 Tip: put a shortcut in your shell profile:

  alias pgenv='source <(playground secrets env)'

options.description: 📄 Example script (default is the last example ran)
📦 Export the whole profile, not only what the example needs
🙈 Print to a terminal anyway, showing every value in clear
🗂️ Secrets profile to use (default is the active one)

subcommands.name: import
subcommands.description:
📥 Import an existing secret.properties / variable.properties file

Each KEY=value line is classified and stored in the right place. A
leading 'export', comments, blank lines and one level of surrounding
quotes are handled; anything that is not an uppercase variable name is
skipped and reported.

This is the one step migration away from 'source secret.properties'.

options.description:
📄 File to import

Required: ✓ Yes
🔥 Securely delete the source file after a successful import

🔐 Treat every line as a credential, whatever the variable names are

Conflicts with: --plain

📝 Treat every line as a non sensitive variable

That is what a variables.properties file usually is: regions, project
ids, account names, URLs.

Conflicts with: --secret
🗂️ Secrets profile to use (default is the active one)

subcommands.name: export
subcommands.description:
📤 Write every credential of a profile to a file, in clear text

❗ Only for the rare case where a tool needs a properties file ❗

The file is written with mode 0600, and a path inside the repository is
refused: it would be one 'git add -A' away from being committed.

🎓 Tip: to feed a shell instead of a file, 'playground secrets env' is
what you want, it exports without writing anything to disk.

options.description:
📄 Destination file, outside the repository

Required: ✓ Yes
🔓 Required, this writes credentials in clear text

🎯 Export only the credentials, only the plain variables, or both

Default value: all
Allowed values: secret, plain, all
🗂️ Secrets profile to use (default is the active one)

subcommands.name: edit
subcommands.description:
✏️ Open the store in your editor

secrets.ini by default, env.ini with --plain. Unless the backend is
file, secrets.ini holds references and not values, so this is where you
rename a variable or move one between profiles, not where you read a
password.

Uses the config key editor, then the EDITOR environment variable, then
vi.

options.description: 📝 Edit the non sensitive variables instead of the secrets

subcommands.name: backend
subcommands.description:
🏦 Show or change where secrets are kept

  keychain     macOS Keychain, through 'security'
  secret-tool  freedesktop secret service (GNOME Keyring, KWallet)
  pass         the standard unix password manager
  op           1Password, through the 'op' CLI
  vault        HashiCorp Vault, through the 'vault' CLI
  file         clear text in secrets.ini, no encryption, last resort

With no configuration, the first available of keychain (macOS),
secret-tool and pass is used, and file is the fallback. op and vault
have to be chosen here, so that an example never blocks on an unlock
prompt halfway through.

Only new values are affected: what is already stored keeps being read
from, and rotated in, the backend it went to.

vault is reference-only, playground never writes to it: create the
secret there, then use 'playground secrets link'. op creates the item
for you, named kdp-<profile>-<NAME> in the vault set by
'playground config set secrets.op-vault' (default: Private), and can
also point at an existing one with 'playground secrets link'.

subcommands.name: profile
subcommands.description:
🗂️ Show or switch the active profile

A profile is an independent set of variables. Without an argument it
lists them all with their variable count, and marks the active one.

A variable missing from the active profile is looked up in 'default',
so what is shared between all of them (CONFLUENT_LICENSE,
NGROK_AUTH_TOKEN) only needs to be stored once, there.

Switching is persistent, it writes the config key secrets.profile. To
use another one just for a command, every secrets command takes
--profile.

🎓 Tip: use one profile per support case, so last week's customer
credentials never leak into this week's reproduction model.

subcommands.name: scan
subcommands.description:
🔎 Look for stored credentials in clear text in the repository

Resolves every credential of the profile and greps the working tree,
tracked and untracked files alike, for the values themselves. Catches
the password pasted into a reproduction model, which no pattern based
scanner would recognise.

Plain variables are skipped, a region or a bucket name is expected to
appear in an example, and so are values shorter than 8 characters,
which would match everywhere. Exits 1 as soon as one is found.

🎓 Tip: wire it as a pre-commit hook with
'playground secrets scan --staged'

options.description: 📦 Scan the staged diff instead of the whole working tree
🗂️ Secrets profile to use (default is the active one)

subcommands.name: salesforce
subcommands.description:
☁️ Set up a Salesforce org for the Salesforce examples, and check it

  setup   configure an org: External Client App (JWT bearer), Platform Event, Change Data Capture
  check   verify that the stored credentials can log in, and that the org has what the examples need

Replaces the manual steps of the Salesforce example READMEs. Only signing
up for the Developer Edition org stays manual.

📖 Step by step guide (Salesforce CLI install, second org, troubleshooting):
https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/salesforce

subcommands.name: setup
subcommands.description:
🛠️ Configure a Salesforce org for the Salesforce examples

Deploys, with the Salesforce CLI (sf) installed on your machine:

  • an External Client App with the OAuth JWT bearer flow, trusting the
    certificate of your keystore, pre-authorized for the profile of your
    user (no browser approval) and with IP restrictions relaxed
  • the Platform Event MyPlatformEvent__e with the text field Message__c
  • Change Data Capture on Contact

then reads the consumer key back, waits until a JWT bearer login works
(a new app takes 2 to 10 minutes to be active), and stores
SALESFORCE_USERNAME, SALESFORCE_INSTANCE and
SALESFORCE_CONSUMER_KEY_WITH_JWT with 'playground secrets set'.

Without --target-org, 'sf org login web' opens the browser once to log
in: that is the only manual step. Running it again on the same org
changes nothing.

🔐 Your keystore (JWT private key and certificate, password confluent)
is ~/.config/kafka-docker-playground/salesforce-confluent.keystore.jks,
outside the repository, and is copied into the Salesforce example
folders, where the examples read it. The first time, the command
reuses the keystore already in the examples if there is one (so the
orgs that trust it keep working), else generates a key pair that never
leaves your machine.

SALESFORCE_PASSWORD and SALESFORCE_SECURITY_TOKEN can't be read from
Salesforce: the command tells you how to store them.

🎓 Tip: use --suffix KDP_CDC (or --account2 for the second org of the
sink examples) to store the per-test variables read by
salesforce_use_test_creds.

options.description:
🔑 Alias or username of an org the sf CLI is already logged into

Without it, 'sf org login web' opens the browser to log in.

🏷️ Alias given to the org by 'sf org login web' (ignored with --target-org)

Default value: kdp-salesforce

🌐 Login URL, stored as SALESFORCE_INSTANCE

https://test.salesforce.com for a sandbox.

Default value: https://login.salesforce.com

📛 API name of the External Client App

Default value: kdp_jwt
🧩 Store the variables with this suffix, e.g. KDP_CDC gives SALESFORCE_USERNAME_KDP_CDC
2️⃣ Store the variables of the second org (SALESFORCE_USERNAME_ACCOUNT2…), used by the sink examples

🔐 PKCS12 keystore (password confluent) holding the JWT private key and certificate

setup: it becomes your keystore (~/.config/kafka-docker-playground/salesforce-confluent.keystore.jks),
copied into the Salesforce example folders.
check: default is your keystore, else connect/connect-salesforce-cdc-source/salesforce-confluent.keystore.jks.

🆕 Generate a new key pair, even if you already have a keystore

The previous one is kept as .bak: the orgs set up with it must be set up again.

⏳ Max seconds to wait for the JWT bearer login to work after the deploy (default 600)

Default value: 600
🧪 Only render the metadata in /tmp/playground-salesforce-setup, deploy and store nothing
🚫 Print the values instead of storing them with 'playground secrets set'

subcommands.name: check
subcommands.description:
🩺 Check that the stored Salesforce credentials work

Logs in with the OAuth JWT bearer flow, exactly like a connector with
salesforce.grant.type=JWT_BEARER (stored SALESFORCE_USERNAME,
SALESFORCE_CONSUMER_KEY_WITH_JWT, SALESFORCE_INSTANCE and the keystore),
explains a rejection, then checks that the org has MyPlatformEvent__e and
Change Data Capture on Contact (warnings: only some examples need them).
Needs neither Docker nor the sf CLI.

Exits with 1 when the login fails.

2️⃣ Store the variables of the second org (SALESFORCE_USERNAME_ACCOUNT2…), used by the sink examples

subcommands.name: cloud-resources
subcommands.description:
☁️ What the playground left behind in your cloud accounts, and what it costs

Examples that talk to a real cloud create real resources, and an
interrupted run leaves them behind. These commands show what is still
alive and what you are being billed for:

  cloud-resources aws list            resources still up, scoped to you
  cloud-resources aws costs           spend over a range of dates
  cloud-resources aws costs-history   spend per month over the last year

The same three exist for azure.

🧹 Nothing is deleted here. To actually remove the resources, use
   'playground cleanup-cloud-resources'.

subcommands.name: aws
subcommands.description:
☁️ What is still running in AWS, and what it costs

  list            resources created by the playground, still alive
  costs           spend over a range of dates, by service
  costs-history   spend per month over the last year

Uses the credentials and region of your aws CLI. Nothing is deleted
here, use 'playground cleanup-cloud-resources' for that.

subcommands.name: list
subcommands.description:
📋 List all active resources

AWS resources created by the playground and still running, matched on
your username. Anything in the list is still being billed.

subcommands.name: costs
subcommands.description:
💰 Show aws costs

Spend over a range of dates, broken down by AWS service, using the
Cost Explorer API. Run it after a week of heavy examples to see which
service the money actually went to, then use
'playground cloud-resources aws list' to find what is still up.

Defaults cover the last month, ending 3 days ago because AWS needs a
couple of days to consolidate. --start-date cannot go back more than
one year.

options.description:
🗓️ start date in format yyyy-mm-dd

Default is 30 days ago

🗓️ end date in format yyyy-mm-dd

  Default is 3 days ago

subcommands.name: costs-history
subcommands.description:
👛  Retrieve aws costs for each month since last year

One line per month over the past year, drawn as a histogram, which
makes a month that went wrong obvious at a glance. Use costs when you
then want to know which service it was.

By default it will only display total cost in dollars. Use the --detailed flag to see more information.

🌐 Also writes a self-contained HTML report in --output-dir, opened in the browser in an interactive terminal (--no-open to skip): cost per month, per service and usage type, the month x service matrix, the top usage types, and the details of each month.

🪣 When S3 costs something, the report adds the Amazon S3 details: cost and volume (GB, requests) of each kind of S3 usage per month (storage, requests, Standard-IA retrieval, data sent to the Internet or to another region), the S3 buckets tagged cflt_managed_id=<user> (region, size per storage class, objects, access logging, lifecycle) and hints. Cost Explorer has no cost per bucket: that needs the resource-level data of the payer account.

options.description: 💹 display all details for each month

📂 Output directory for the HTML report (default: /tmp/playground-cloud-costs)

Default value: /tmp/playground-cloud-costs
🚫 Do not open the HTML report in the browser

🧪 Sample of tools/cloud-costs/samples: writes the HTML report from this dummy cost data, without calling AWS

To see what the report looks like before running it on your account.

Allowed values: aws_dummy

subcommands.name: azure
subcommands.description:
☁️ What is still running in Azure, and what it costs

  list            resources created by the playground, still alive
  costs           spend over a range of dates
  costs-history   spend per month over the last year

Uses the subscription your az CLI is logged into. Nothing is deleted
here, use 'playground cleanup-cloud-resources' for that.

subcommands.name: list

subcommands.name: run
subcommands.description:
🕹️ Run any example !

🔥 It start an interactive mode where you'll be fully guided !

  playground run                       🔍 pick an example, guided
  playground run -f <example.sh>       🚀 run that one directly
  playground re-run                    ⚡ same example, same flags

Each run stops what was running, starts the environment the example asks
for, brings up its containers, creates the connector and produces data.
Credentials the example needs are loaded from 'playground secrets'.

🔢 Choosing versions
  --tag             Confluent Platform version for every component
  --connect-tag     Confluent Platform version for connect only
  --schema-registry-tag, --ksqldb-tag, --control-center-tag
                    version for that component only
  --connector-tag   connector version from Confluent Hub
  --connector-zip   connector from a local zip or a URL
  --connector-jar   a single jar, dropped into the existing plugin

🧰 Adding to the example
  --environment     run a connector example under another security setup
  --enable-<x>      add control-center, ksqldb, flink, grafana, kcat...
  --enable-sql-datagen
                    continuous realistic data for CDC source examples
  --benchmark       benchmark the connector once the example succeeded
  --connect-community-image, --kafka-community-image
                    use community images instead of enterprise ones
  --enable-kraft    KRaft instead of Zookeeper for CP 7.4 to 7.9
  --connect-log-level
                    log levels set on connect before the connector is created


⛅ When running Confluent Cloud (ccloud) example:

  All you have to do is to be already logged in with confluent CLI.

  By default, a new Confluent Cloud environment with a Cluster will be created.

  You can configure the new cluster by setting:

  --cluster-type (or CLUSTER_TYPE environment variable): The type of cluster (possible values: basic, standard and dedicated, default basic)
  --cluster-cloud (or CLUSTER_CLOUD environment variable): The Cloud provider (possible values: aws, gcp and azure, default aws)
  --cluster-region (or CLUSTER_REGION environment variable): The Cloud region (use confluent kafka region list to get the list, default eu-west-2 for aws, westeurope for azure and europe-west2 for gcp)
  --cluster-environment (or ENVIRONMENT environment variable) (optional): The environment id where want your new cluster (example: txxxxx) 

  In case you want to use your own existing cluster, you need to setup, in addition to previous ones:

  --cluster-name (or CLUSTER_NAME environment variable): The cluster name
  --cluster-creds (or CLUSTER_CREDS environment variable): The Kafka api key and secret to use, it should be separated with colon (example: <API_KEY>:<API_KEY_SECRET>)
  --cluster-schema-registry-creds (or SCHEMA_REGISTRY_CREDS environment variable) (optional, if not set, new one will be created): The Schema Registry api key and secret to use, it should be separated with colon (example: <SR_API_KEY>:<SR_API_KEY_SECRET>)

📄 Run log
  The output is also written to a text file, passwords, api keys and
  tokens masked, ready to share with a colleague: the
  command to re-run, the versions, the host, the result and, for a
  failure, the errors of the connect container. Its path is printed at
  the end of the run. The last 50 are kept in
  /tmp/playground-run-logs.

  --run-log-file    write it to that file
  --no-run-log      don't write it
  playground config run-log false | run-log-folder <folder>

  The masking is best-effort: review the file before sharing it
  outside Confluent.

❗ this command will kill all containers using "playground container kill-all", you can disable this by running "playground config container-kill-all-before-run false"

🍪 Deep dive: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/deep-dive-run-and-versions
🎬 Bite size session: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/sessions?id=%F0%9F%95%B9%EF%B8%8F-run-an-example-with-the-menu-or-with-flags

options.description:
🔐 The environment to start when running a connector example 

- plaintext
- ccloud
- cfk
- cfk-rbac
- 2way-ssl
- kerberos
- ldap-authorizer-sasl-plain
- ldap-sasl-plain
- rbac-sasl-plain
- sasl-plain
- sasl-scram
- sasl-ssl
- ssl_kerberos

Default is plaintext.
This is only supported when example is a connector example

Default value: plaintext
Allowed values: ccloud, cfk, cfk-rbac, plaintext, sasl-ssl, sasl-plain, 2way-ssl, sasl-scram, kerberos, ssl_kerberos, ldap-authorizer-sasl-plain, ldap-sasl-plain, rbac-sasl-plain

🔖 Example file to run

❕ It must be absolute full path

🎓 Tip: use <tab> completion to trigger fzf completion
📖 Opening example files (including docker-compose file) with text editor set with playground config editor <editor> (default is code)

🎯 Confluent Platform (CP) version to use. Applies to all components (broker, connect, schema registry, ksqlDB, etc...)

It sets TAG environment variable

Must be greater or equal to 5.3.0

🎓 Tip: use <tab> completion to trigger fzf completion

🔗 Confluent Platform (CP) version to use. Applies to connect only.

It sets CP_CONNECT_TAG environment variable

Must be greater or equal to 5.3.0

🎓 Tip: use <tab> completion to trigger fzf completion

🔰 Confluent Platform (CP) version to use for schema registry only

It sets CP_SCHEMA_REGISTRY_TAG environment variable

❗ not supported with ccloud examples (schema registry is in Confluent Cloud)

🎓 Tip: use <tab> completion to trigger fzf completion

🎏 Confluent Platform (CP) version to use for ksqlDB server and CLI only, with --enable-ksqldb

It sets CP_KSQL_TAG and CP_KSQL_CLI_TAG environment variables

❗ not supported with ccloud examples

🎓 Tip: use <tab> completion to trigger fzf completion

💠 Control Center version to use, with --enable-control-center

It sets CP_CONTROL_CENTER_TAG environment variable

With Control Center Next Gen (default), this is the version of the confluentinc/cp-enterprise-control-center-next-gen image (for example 2.2.0, default is latest)

With --enable-legacy-control-center, this is a CP version (< 8), by default the one of --tag

🔗 Connector version to use

By default, for each connector, the latest available version on Confluent Hub is used

🎓 Tip: set to " " in order to select the version dynamically (for Confluent plugins, the preview shows the release notes of each version)

Conflicts with: --connector-zip

🤐 Connector zip to use

❕ It must be absolute full path

🎓 Tip: use <tab> completion to trigger fzf completion 
        use playground config folder_zip_or_jar <folder1> <folder2>... (default is home folder and current folder is always included) to configure where to search the files
        use <option+enter> to use the value you typed manually

Conflicts with: --connector-tag

🤎 Connector jar to use

❕ It must be absolute full path

🎓 Tip: use <tab> completion to trigger fzf completion 
        use playground config folder_zip_or_jar <folder1> <folder2>... (default is home folder and current folder is always included) to configure where to search the files
        use <option+enter> to use the value you typed manually

🚀 Enable ksqlDB 

❗ not supported with ccloud examples

By default, ksqldb-server and ksqldb-cli containers are not started for every test

🧲 Enable Rest Proxy

❗ not supported with ccloud examples

By default, rest-proxy container is not started for every test

💠 Enable Control Center

By default, control-center container is not started for every test

Control Center is reachable at http://127.0.0.1:9021

🐿️ Enable Flink

By default, flink is not started for every test

Once enabled, the CLI will ask if you need to download any connectors. Based on the response, you can download one or more connectors from Flink maven repository.

To skip the question (in a script or CI), set FLINK_URL to the jar(s) to download, e.g. the Kafka SQL connector.

Flink UI and REST API: http://127.0.0.1:18081

🎓 Tip: run Flink SQL and manage the jobs with 'playground flink sql|list-jobs|cancel', see the flink/flink-sql-kafka example.

🐺 Enable Conduktor Platform

By default, Conduktor Platform container is not started for every test

Conduktor is reachable at http://127.0.0.1:8080/console (admin/admin)

3️⃣ Enable multiple brokers

By default, there is only one broker node enabled. With 3 brokers (ids
1, 2 and 3), the internal topics (consumer offsets, transactions,
connect, schemas, license...) have 3 replicas and a min ISR of 2, like
in production: a broker can stop without making them unavailable.

🥉 Enable multiple connect worker node

By default, there is only one connect worker node enabled

Enable Grafana, Prometheus and Pyroscope

📊 Grafana is reachable at http://127.0.0.1:3000 (login/password is admin/password)

🛡️ Prometheus is reachable at http://127.0.0.1:9090

📛 Pyroscope is reachable at http://127.0.0.1:4040

🐈‍⬛ Enable kcat

You can use it with:

$ docker exec kcat kcat -b broker:9092 -L

🌪️ Enable SQL Datagen injection

Once the example succeeded, rows are injected with the benchmark-load.bash next to the example script (the load of
playground connector benchmark): one row per transaction, in parallel sessions, for a few minutes, while Grafana shows
the connector. Works with the JDBC, Debezium, Oracle CDC and XStream source examples (Oracle, MySQL, MariaDB,
PostgreSQL, SQL Server), self-managed and fully managed, and with their reproduction models.

SQL_DATAGEN_DURATION (minutes, default 10) and SQL_DATAGEN_SESSIONS (default 5) change the duration and the number of
parallel sessions, BENCHMARK_LOAD_SCRIPT another load script than benchmark-load.bash (see playground connector
benchmark).

🏎️ Benchmark the connector once the example succeeded

Runs playground connector benchmark on the connector of the example: a
drain of the load of a source (benchmark-load.bash next to the example
script) or of the records produced by a sink example, then the
throughput, the HTML report and where the task time went. Self-managed
and fully managed connectors, not with the cfk environment.

--benchmark takes no value: the flags of playground connector benchmark
go in the BENCHMARK_ARGS environment variable, for instance a backlog of
10 million records of 100 bytes:

BENCHMARK_ARGS="--nb-records 10000000 --record-size 100" playground run -f csv.sh --benchmark

or a steady run: BENCHMARK_ARGS="--mode steady --duration 5m".
BENCHMARK_LOAD_SCRIPT selects another load script than benchmark-load.bash.
If the benchmark fails, the command exits with its exit code.

📄 Write the masked log of this run to this file, instead of the run log folder

Same file as the one written by default (see 'playground config run-log'), at this path.

Conflicts with: --no-run-log

🙈 Don't write the masked log of this run (see 'playground config run-log')

Conflicts with: --run-log-file

🌱 Use the community connect image (confluentinc/cp-kafka-connect) instead of the enterprise one (confluentinc/cp-server-connect)

It sets CP_CONNECT_IMAGE environment variable

Monitoring interceptors are disabled, as they are not part of the community image

🌿 Use the community kafka image (confluentinc/cp-kafka) instead of the enterprise one (confluentinc/cp-server)

It sets CP_KAFKA_IMAGE environment variable

Confluent Metrics Reporter and Telemetry Reporter are disabled, as they are not part of the community image

🛰️ Start Confluent Platform in KRaft mode

It sets ENABLE_KRAFT environment variable

Only useful for CP versions from 7.4 to 7.9, where Zookeeper is used by default (KRaft is always used for CP >= 8)

👨‍🦳 Use legacy Control Center (confluentinc/cp-enterprise-control-center) instead of Control Center Next Gen

It sets ENABLE_LEGACY_CONTROL_CENTER environment variable

Legacy Control Center is not available for CP >= 8. It implies --enable-control-center

🔊 Log level(s) to set on connect, as a comma separated list of <package>=<level> (level is one of INFO, WARN, DEBUG, TRACE)

They are applied with 'playground debug log-level set' as soon as the environment is started and connect is ready, so before the example creates its connector

Example: --connect-log-level "io.confluent.connect.s3=TRACE,org.apache.kafka.connect.runtime.WorkerSinkTask=DEBUG"

🌤 The cloud provider: aws, gcp or azure. Default is aws

🎓 Tip: you can also use CLUSTER_CLOUD environment variable

Allowed values: aws, gcp, azure

🔋 The cluster type: basic, standard or dedicated. Default is basic

🎓 Tip: you can also use CLUSTER_TYPE environment variable

Allowed values: basic, standard, dedicated

🗺 The Cloud region. 

🎓 Tip: you can also use CLUSTER_REGION environment variable
🎓 Tip: use <tab> completion to trigger fzf completion

🌐 The environment id where want your new cluster (example: txxxxx)

ℹ️ Optional, if not set, new environment will be created

🎓 Tip: you can also use ENVIRONMENT environment variable
🎓 Tip: use <tab> completion to trigger fzf completion

🎰 The cluster name. 

❣️ Only required if you want to use your own existing cluster

🎓 Tip: you can also use CLUSTER_NAME environment variable
🎓 Tip: use <tab> completion to trigger fzf completion

🔒 The Kafka api key and secret to use, it should be separated with colon (example: <API_KEY>:<API_KEY_SECRET>)

❣️ Only required if you want to use your own existing cluster

🎓 Tip: you can also use CLUSTER_CREDS environment variable

🔒 The Schema Registry api key and secret to use, it should be separated with colon (example: <SR_API_KEY>:<SR_API_KEY_SECRET>)

ℹ️ Optional, if not set, new credentials will be created

❣️ Only required if you want to use your own existing cluster

🎓 Tip: you can also use SCHEMA_REGISTRY_CREDS environment variable

👤 Run the fully managed connectors with a service account (kafka.auth.mode=SERVICE_ACCOUNT)

Instead of the API key of the example, each fully managed or custom
connector gets its own service account, with the ACLs listed in
https://docs.confluent.io/cloud/current/connectors/service-account.html
(derived from the connector config), and the owner of
CONFLUENT_CLOUD_API_KEY gets the Assigner role on it. The example is
not changed.

The service accounts and their ACLs are deleted with the connectors
(playground connector delete, end-of-run cleanup, playground
cleanup-cloud-resources).

🎓 Tip: to reproduce an authorization error, delete or deny an ACL with
playground rbac acl delete|create --connector <connector> [--deny],
restart the connector and run playground connector diagnose.
PG_CCLOUD_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_ACL_EXCLUDE skips ACLs when they are created.

🎬 Bite size session: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/sessions?id=%F0%9F%91%A4-a-fully-managed-connector-with-a-service-account-loses-an-acl

🚦 ACLs of the service accounts created by --ccloud-service-account (implies it)

  docs  the ACLs of the documentation, derived from the connector config (default)
  full  every operation on every topic, group and transactional id (same as the API key of the example)
  none  no ACL, add them with playground rbac acl create --connector <connector>

Allowed values: docs, full, none

👤 Use this existing service account (sa-xxxxx) for the fully managed connectors, as is (implies --ccloud-service-account)

No ACL is created nor deleted, and the service account is kept.

subcommands.name: re-run
subcommands.description:
⚡ Simply re-run last example you ran with <playground run>

Same script and same flags as last time: the --tag, --connector-tag,
--connector-zip and --enable-* you picked are replayed from playground.ini,
so there is nothing to retype after a code change.

🎓 Tip: to re-run with a different version, use 'playground run' again and
change the flag, or 'playground update-version' on the running example.

🍪 Deep dive: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/deep-dive-run-and-versions
🎬 Bite size session: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/sessions?id=%F0%9F%95%B9%EF%B8%8F-run-an-example-with-the-menu-or-with-flags

subcommands.name: get-ci-result
subcommands.description:
🤖 get CI result for current example

Tells you whether the example you are running is green in the nightly CI,
both for the default environment and for cfk, by reading the published
badges from kafka-docker-playground.io.

👉 Useful before you spend time debugging: if CI is red too, the breakage
is probably not on your side. Reproduction models are always reported as
fine, they are not part of the CI matrix.

🔥 With --logs, also tells why it is red: the latest failing CI job of the
example is located from its '🔥' GitHub issue, its full log is downloaded,
and for each failing script the last lines before the failure are shown
with a digest of the ERROR/FATAL records (same digest as 'playground
container logs --errors').

🌐 With --logs, also writes a self-contained HTML report of the failure in --output-dir, opened in the browser in an interactive terminal (--no-open to skip): known causes, last lines before the failure of each failing script, root causes and every distinct record, with links to the issue and the job.

Use --test to ask about any example, without running it.

options.description:
📂 Example directory (or script) to check, instead of the current example

Examples: connect/connect-aws-s3-sink, other/connect-secret-registry

🔐 CI environment to check: plaintext or cfk

Default is the environment of the current example, or plaintext with --test

Allowed values: plaintext, cfk
🦭 Check the podman CI run instead of the docker one
🔥 When CI is red, show why: tail and ERROR/FATAL digest of each failing script of the latest failing job

✂️ With --logs, maximum number of distinct records to show per failing script (default 20). The HTML report has them all

Default value: 20

📂 With --logs, output directory for the HTML report (default: /tmp/playground-ci-result)

Default value: /tmp/playground-ci-result
🙈 With --logs, do not open the HTML report in the browser

🏰 Get an history of the examples which were run with run command and run it again

Opens a picker over every 'playground run' command you have executed,
most recent first and de-duplicated. The command you select is shown for
editing before it runs, so you can change a --tag or add a flag on the way.

🍪 Deep dive: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/deep-dive-run-and-versions
🎬 Bite size session: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/sessions?id=%F0%9F%95%B9%EF%B8%8F-run-an-example-with-the-menu-or-with-flags

subcommands.name: find-example
subcommands.description:
🔎 Find examples matching a free-text query, without the interactive picker

Searches every runnable example script (connect/, ccloud/, ksqldb/,
flink/, reproduction-models/, ...) by path, connector class, README title
and script body. Every word of the query must match somewhere; matches in
the path and connector class rank higher than matches in the body.

Prints the ready-to-paste 'playground run -f' command for each hit, best
first. Use 'playground run' instead to browse examples interactively.

options.description:
📂 Restrict the search to one top-level folder

Allowed values: connect, ccloud, ksqldb, flink, schema-registry, rest-proxy, multi-data-center, other, operator, academy, environment, reproduction-models

🔢 Maximum number of hits (default 10)

Default value: 10

📗 Print the hits as a JSON array, best first, and nothing else

Each hit has script (absolute path), path (relative to the repository),
title (README), connector_classes, environment, score and run_command.
No hit prints [] and exits with code 1.

🎓 Tip: use it in scripts and from AI agents, for example with
jq -r '.[0].script'

subcommands.name: switch-ccloud
subcommands.description:
🌩️  Switch to ccloud environment.

It will bootstrap ccloud environment based on your previously ran ccloud example.

Points the CLI at the Confluent Cloud cluster of your last ccloud run, so
that 'playground topic', 'playground connector' and 'playground schema'
talk to Confluent Cloud instead of the local containers. Nothing is
created or destroyed, and no container is started or stopped.

❕ Requires that you ran a ccloud example at least once, so that the
   environment, cluster and credentials are cached in playground.ini.
   The environment you were on is remembered for 'playground switch-back'.

subcommands.name: switch-back
subcommands.description:
💺  Switch back from previous environment before switch-ccloud was called.

Restores the environment and connector type that were active before
'playground switch-ccloud', so the CLI talks to your local containers
again.

subcommands.name: switch-podman
subcommands.description:
🦭 Switch the container engine to Podman

Points the 'docker' CLI, 'docker compose' and the playground at the rootful
Podman socket, through a 'podman' docker context: the switch applies to your
current shell and to new ones, with nothing to export. On macOS the podman
machine is started if needed. Ends with 'playground doctor'.

Containers are not moved between engines: stop the running example first.

❕ Podman must be set up once, see
   https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/how-to-use?id=🦭-using-podman-instead-of-docker
   The docker context you were on is remembered for 'playground switch-docker'.

subcommands.name: switch-docker
subcommands.description:
🐳 Switch the container engine back to Docker

Restores the docker context that was active before 'playground switch-podman'
(Docker Desktop's 'desktop-linux', or 'default', if none was remembered).
Ends with 'playground doctor'.

Containers are not moved between engines: stop the running example first.

subcommands.name: update-version
subcommands.description:
✨ Update current confluent platform components (all with --tag or only connect with --connect-tag) or connector(s) with new version(s)

Re-runs the example you are currently on with different versions, which is
the fastest way to answer "does it still happen on 8.x?" or "is it fixed in
connector 10.6.0?".

  --tag            🔢 every Confluent Platform component
  --connect-tag    🔗 only the connect container, other components untouched
  --connector-tag  🧩 the connector, from Confluent Hub
  --connector-zip  📦 the connector, from a local zip or a URL
  --connector-jar  ☕ a single jar, dropped into the existing plugin

With no flag, you are prompted with the versions available. The versions
currently running are read from the broker and connect containers, so the
example must be up.

🎓 Tip: this is a version bisect tool. Keep the example running and call it
repeatedly until you find the version where the behaviour changes.

🍪 Deep dive: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/deep-dive-run-and-versions
🎬 Bite size session: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/sessions?id=%F0%9F%8E%AF-is-it-fixed-in-a-newer-version

subcommands.name: repro
subcommands.description:
👷‍♂️ Reproduction model commands

A reproduction model is an example written to demonstrate one specific
problem, so that anyone can reproduce it with a single command.

  bootstrap   scaffold one from an existing example, then edit it
  list        find models by case, status, verdict, base example, author, date
  diff        what a model changes compared with its base example
  status      show or update what a model proves: expected, actual, jira, status
  assert      end a model with its verdict: 🐞 reproduced or ✅ not reproduced
  bisect      run a model on several versions: which one introduced or fixed it
  export      package one or more models as a self-contained tgz bundle
  import      unpack a bundle someone sent you, and run it
  check       scan models for secrets and customer data before committing them

👉 Always scaffold with bootstrap rather than copying a script by hand: it
creates the header, the docker compose override, the CLI cheat sheet and
registers the model, which a hand-written file would be missing.

Keep a model minimal and about one issue, state expected versus actual
behaviour in its header (🎯 expected / 💥 actual), and never put customer
data in it.

🍪 Deep dive: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/deep-dive-reproduction-models
🎬 Bite size session: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/sessions?id=%F0%9F%A7%AA-the-life-of-a-reproduction-model

subcommands.name: export
subcommands.description:
📤 Export reproduction models as a self-contained tgz bundle

Produces a single tgz that a colleague can feed to
'playground repro import' to run your scenario as is.

The bundle holds what the model needs, committed or not: the script,
the files of its folder it mentions (docker compose override, producer,
SQL files…) and the support files linked by bootstrap (README.md,
stop.sh, benchmark-load.bash, config-*). Symlinks are stored as their
content, so the bundle does not depend on the version of the base
example. Git-ignored files, build output (target/), dumps, flight
recordings, logs and credential files (keyfile.json, *.pem, *.key) are
left out.

A repro-manifest.json describes the bundle: the last 'playground run'
line of each model (from playground-run-history), its case number,
author, base example, the playground commit, the names (never the
values) of the credentials it needs, and the sha256 of every file.

Before anything is written, the bundle is scanned. The export stops
(unless --force) when a file contains the value of a credential known
to this machine ('playground secrets' store, exported credential
variables, CLUSTER_CREDS / SCHEMA_REGISTRY_CREDS of playground.ini,
~/.aws/credentials) or a well-known token format (AWS access key id,
private key, GitHub / Slack token, Google API key, JWT, Azure storage
account key). Email addresses, public IP addresses and hard-coded
passwords that do not come from the base example are reported as
possible customer data. Values are never printed.

Files outside the repository that a model needs (--connector-zip /
--connector-jar of its run line, files whose absolute path appears in
the script or its compose files, like ~/Downloads/config.json) are
only listed, unless --include-artifacts packs them under
<model folder>/artifacts/. Import then points the run line, the script
and the compose files to the imported copies. Import also rewrites the
paths of the exporter's checkout (like the jar path written by
'repro bootstrap --custom-smt') to the local ones.

--cluster-creds / --cluster-schema-registry-creds are removed from the
run line: whoever imports runs with their own cluster.

Without --file, the current reproduction model is exported.

📖 Each model gets a hand-off report, <model>.REPRO.md next to its
script in the bundle: case, jira, status, last verdict, 🎯 expected,
💥 actual, the commands to import and run it, the credentials it
needs, and what it changes compared with the script of its base
example (diff). 'playground repro import' prints where it is.
--report-only prints it (Markdown, for a Jira or a Slack message)
without writing the bundle, --no-report leaves it out.

📋 On macOS, the bundle is copied to the clipboard as a file: paste it
(Cmd+V) in a Slack conversation to attach it (--no-clipboard to skip).

🎓 Tip: start with --dry-run to see what would be packed, and what the scan finds.
The same scan runs on commits with 'playground repro check'.

Can be repeated to put several models in one bundle.

Repeatable: ✓ Yes
Conflicts with: --all-uncommitted, --all

subcommands.name: check
subcommands.description:
🕵️ Scan reproduction models for secrets and customer data before they are committed

Runs the scan of 'playground repro export' on the files of the
reproduction models, without packing anything. It stops (exit code 1)
when a file contains the value of a credential known to this machine
('playground secrets' store, exported credential variables,
CLUSTER_CREDS / SCHEMA_REGISTRY_CREDS of playground.ini,
~/.aws/credentials) or a well-known token format (AWS access key id,
private key, GitHub / Slack token, Google API key, JWT, Azure storage
account key), and when a credential file (keyfile.json, *.pem, *.key,
*.p12, *.jks, secrets.properties, playground.ini) is about to be
committed. Email addresses, public IP addresses, hard-coded passwords
that do not come from the base example, and dumps, logs or archives
are reported as possible customer data, without failing. Values are
never printed.

Without flag, the new and modified files of reproduction-models are
checked. Symlinks to the public examples are not.

🪝 'playground repro bootstrap' and 'playground repro import' set up a
pre-commit hook in reproduction-models (git config core.hooksPath
<playground>/scripts/repro-git-hooks) that runs
'playground repro check --staged --skip-secrets-store' on every commit.
An existing pre-commit hook or core.hooksPath is never replaced. To skip
the scan of one commit: git commit --no-verify, or
PLAYGROUND_REPRO_SCAN=skip git commit. PLAYGROUND_REPRO_SCAN=full also
reads the 'playground secrets' store.

subcommands.name: import
subcommands.description:
📥 Import a tgz bundle created by 'playground repro export'

The bundle is extracted to a temporary folder first and checked: no
absolute paths, no '..', no special files, and the sha256 of every file
must match its manifest. Bundles from older versions, without manifest,
are still accepted.

Files identical to yours are skipped. When a file differs, the import
stops unless --on-conflict says what to do. Files that were symlinks to
a public example are restored as symlinks when the public file is
identical, otherwise their content is kept.

Then the model becomes the current one, and the command prints the
'playground run' line to use and the credentials missing from your
'playground secrets' profile. --run goes on with that line when
nothing is missing (in a terminal, it asks first when containers are
running: the run stops them).

--file also takes a URL (a GitHub release asset, a raw file, any public
link): the bundle is downloaded into an empty temporary folder, then
checked like a local one. Links that need a login (Slack, Google
Drive) must be downloaded by hand.

🤐 Bundle file (playground_repro_*.tgz, any name is accepted), or its https:// URL

🎓 Tip: use <tab> completion to trigger fzf completion
        use playground config folder_zip_or_jar <folder1> <folder2>... (default is home folder and current folder is always included) to configure where to search the files

Required: ✓ Yes

⚔️ What to do when a file of the bundle differs from your copy

abort: import nothing and list the differences
rename: import the differing files with an -imported-<date> suffix (references in the imported scripts are updated)
overwrite: replace your copy

Default value: abort
Allowed values: abort, rename, overwrite

subcommands.name: status
subcommands.description:
🩹 Show or update what a reproduction model proves, from its header

'playground repro bootstrap' writes these fields under '# 💬 comments:'
in the header of the model, one line each:

  # 🎯 expected: what should happen
  # 💥 actual: what happens instead (the problem)
  # 🎫 jira: the Jira of the problem
  # 🩹 status: open, fixed in <version>, not a bug, customer config…

Without flag, prints the fields with the description, case, author and
base example (--json for scripts). With --set, --expected, --actual or
--jira, updates the lines, then prints them. A model created before the
fields existed gets the missing lines added after '# 💬 comments:'.

'playground repro export' copies the fields into repro-manifest.json,
and 'playground repro import' prints them.

Without --file, the current reproduction model is used.

the example. The compose override renamed by bootstrap
(docker-compose.plaintext.repro-<description>.yml) is compared under
the name of the example's, so that line is not reported.

and removed (from the 'playground connector create-or-update'
heredocs), then the diffs (in color in a terminal).

The hand-off report of 'playground repro export' has the same diffs.

Without --file, the current reproduction model is used.

example, whether it is committed, and the last verdict recorded by
'playground repro assert'. A model without a date in its header gets

🧪 End a reproduction model with its verdict: 🐞 REPRODUCED or ✅ NOT REPRODUCED

Put it at the end of the scenario, with the check that says the
problem is there (the 💥 actual of the header). It prints the verdict
with the CP and connector versions, and records it in
playground-repro-verdicts (a local file of the repository root, not
committed), so that it can be compared between runs and versions:

  playground repro status     shows the last verdict of the model
  playground repro export     writes it in repro-manifest.json

One check per call (combine several with --reproduced-if-command):

  --reproduced-if-log <pattern>               a line of the logs of
                                              --container (default
                                              connect) matches (grep)
  --reproduced-if-connector-state <state>     the connector or one of
                                              its tasks is in this state
  --reproduced-if-records-less-than <n>       --topic has less records
  --reproduced-if-records-more-than <n>       --topic has more records
  --reproduced-if-command "<command>"         the shell command succeeds

Both verdicts exit with 0: a model that does not reproduce is a result,
not an error. The exit code is 1 only when the check cannot run.

Without --file, the verdict is recorded for the current model (the one
'playground run' runs).

subcommands.name: bisect
subcommands.description:
🔀 Run a reproduction model on several versions: which one introduced or fixed the problem

Runs the model once per version ('playground run -f <model>
--connector-tag <version>', or --tag for CP versions) and reads the
verdict that 'playground repro assert' records at the end of each run.
The model must end with 'playground repro assert'.

  --connector-tag A --connector-tag B …   these connector versions
  --from A --to B                         the Confluent Hub versions of
                                          the connector of the model
                                          between A and B: a binary
                                          search (first, last, then the
                                          middle until the verdict
                                          changes), --all for every one
  --tag A --tag B …                       these CP versions

Prints the verdict of each version (🐞 reproduced, ✅ not reproduced,
❓ no verdict when the run stopped before 'repro assert'), the versions
where it changes and, for a Confluent connector, the changelog between
them ('playground connector-plugin changelog'). The log of each run is
in /tmp/playground-repro-bisect/<model>-<version>.log, the summary in
/tmp/playground-repro-bisect/<model>-<date>.json.

⚠️ Each run stops the running environment, like 'playground run', and a
run takes the time of the model: a binary search over 30 versions is
about 6 runs.

subcommands.name: tcp-proxy
subcommands.description:
🏚 Zazkia TCP Proxy commands

Simulate TCP connection issues (reset,delay,throttle,corrupt) using emicklei/zazkia (https://github.com/emicklei/zazkia) TCP proxy

Slips a controllable proxy between a connector and the system it talks to,
so you can break the connection on purpose and watch what the connector
does: does it retry, does it lose records, does it fail the task.

  start        put the proxy in the path, rewriting the connector config
  delay        add latency to the responses
  break        drop a percentage of the responses
  close-connection, close-all-connection-with-error
  toggle-*     cut reads or writes in one direction only
  get-connections   the live connections and their statistics
  open-ui      drive all of the above from the Zazkia web UI

🎓 Tip: start with 'playground tcp-proxy open-ui' to see what is
happening, then reproduce the same actions from the CLI in a script.

subcommands.name: start
subcommands.description:
💗 Start the TCP proxy and automatically replace connector config with zazkia hostname and port 49998

Starts the proxy in front of --hostname and --port, then rewrites the
running connector configuration so its traffic goes through it. Nothing
else to change on your side.

options.description:
Hostname used by the tcp proxy to forward request

Required: ✓ Yes

Port used by the tcp proxy to forward request

Required: ✓ Yes

🐌 Throttle service response. This is bytes per second.

Default value: 0

⏲️ Add milliseconds delay to service response. Default is 0 ms.

Default value: 0

💔 Percentage of broken connections. Default is 0%.

Default value: 0
🦹‍♂️ Corrupt service response with random mangled bytes. By default, there is no corruption.

🤖 By default, script will attempt to modify automatically the running connector config to use Zazkia proxy.

This flag allows to skip this automatic configuration (only useful if you want to manually update connector config with zazkia tcp proxy details)

subcommands.name: get-connections
subcommands.description:
🧲 Get Zazkia active TCP connections config and stats

Lists every TCP connection currently going through the proxy, with its
id, its state (the toggles and the delay or break currently applied) and
its stats (bytes sent and received each way).

Start here: the id printed by this command is what the other tcp-proxy
commands take as --connection-id. Connections in EOF state are hidden.

🎓 Tip: every other tcp-proxy command applies to all active connections
when you do not pass --connection-id, which is normally what you want.

options.description: 🧲 Zazkia TCP connection id

subcommands.name: delay
subcommands.description:
⏲️ Add milliseconds delay to service response.

Slows down every response coming back from the service, without
breaking anything. This is how you reproduce a slow database or a slow
API: request timeouts, retries, rebalances caused by a task that takes
too long to answer.

Set it back to 0 to remove the delay.

The new state is printed afterwards, so you can check it was applied.

options.description:
⏲️ Add milliseconds delay to service response.

Required: ✓ Yes
🧲 Zazkia TCP connection id

subcommands.name: break
subcommands.description:
💔 Break sending the response to the client.

Drops the response part way through, for the given percentage of
responses. Unlike close-connection, which kills the connection once,
this keeps failing intermittently, which is what you need to reproduce
the flaky network a customer is seeing rather than a clean outage.

Set it back to 0 to stop breaking responses.

The new state is printed afterwards, so you can check it was applied.

options.description:
💔 Percentage of broken connections.

Required: ✓ Yes
🧲 Zazkia TCP connection id

subcommands.name: close-connection
subcommands.description:
❌ Close the Zazkia active TCP connections

Kills the connection abruptly, the way a firewall or a restarted
database would. Use it to check that the connector reconnects on its
own, and how long it takes.

Without --connection-id, every active connection is closed.

options.description: 🧲 Zazkia TCP connection id

subcommands.name: close-all-connection-with-error
subcommands.description:
🧹 Close all Zazkia TCP connections which are in error state

Same as the "close all with error" button in the Zazkia UI. Connections
left behind by a previous break or delay clutter get-connections;
this cleans them up so you only see the live ones.

subcommands.name: toggle-accept-connections
subcommands.description:
🙅‍♂️ Change whether new connections can be accepted

Turn it off and the service looks down to anything trying to connect,
while the connections already open keep working. That is the way to
reproduce a connector that cannot reconnect after a failure, or an
exhausted connection pool.

This is a toggle, run it again to accept connections once more.

subcommands.name: toggle-reads-client
subcommands.description:
✅ Change whether reading data from the client is enabled.

Stops the proxy from reading what the client sends. The client's writes
pile up in its socket buffer and it eventually blocks, which is how you
reproduce backpressure and produce timeouts.

This is a toggle, run it again to restore the flow.

  See diagram in https://github.com/emicklei/zazkia#how-does-it-work- (or locally http://localhost:9191/help.html)

options.description: 🧲 Zazkia TCP connection id

subcommands.name: toggle-reads-service
subcommands.description:
✅ Change whether reading data from the service is enabled.

Stops the proxy from reading what the service replies. Nothing comes
back to the client, so requests hang until they time out, without the
connection ever being closed. This is the classic black hole that a
TCP keepalive misconfiguration produces.

This is a toggle, run it again to restore the flow.

  See diagram in https://github.com/emicklei/zazkia#how-does-it-work- (or locally http://localhost:9191/help.html)

options.description: 🧲 Zazkia TCP connection id

subcommands.name: toggle-writes-client
subcommands.description:
✅ Change whether writing data to the client is enabled.

The proxy keeps reading the service's response but never forwards it to
the client. Close to toggle-reads-service from the client's point of
view, except the service sees its response as fully sent, so both sides
disagree about what happened.

This is a toggle, run it again to restore the flow.

  See diagram in https://github.com/emicklei/zazkia#how-does-it-work- (or locally http://localhost:9191/help.html)

options.description: 🧲 Zazkia TCP connection id

subcommands.name: toggle-writes-service
subcommands.description:
✅ Change whether writing data to the service is enabled.

The proxy keeps reading the client's request but never forwards it to
the service. The client believes it sent its data, the service never
receives it, so nothing ever answers.

This is a toggle, run it again to restore the flow.

  See diagram in https://github.com/emicklei/zazkia#how-does-it-work- (or locally http://localhost:9191/help.html)

options.description: 🧲 Zazkia TCP connection id

subcommands.name: open-ui
subcommands.description:
🌐 Just open Zazkia UI (http://localhost:9191) in your browser

The UI shows the same connections as get-connections, but live, with
the toggles as buttons and a diagram of which direction each one cuts.
Easier than the CLI when you are exploring, the CLI is what you put in
a reproduction script once you know which fault you want.

🧰 Tools commands

Small utilities that are handy around the playground but are not tied to a
running environment:

  read-avro-file        dump an avro file as readable json

  certs-create          generate a keystore and truststore for a component

🪄 Install a slightly modified version of "Shell Script Command Completion" Visual Studio Code extension (https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=tetradresearch.vscode-h2o)

Gives you the same completion inside VS Code as in your terminal: while
editing an example or a reproduction model, playground commands, flags
and their allowed values are proposed as you type, with the help text
on hover. Worth the two minutes of setup if you write example scripts.

  flight-recorder         JFR: where the time of the connector tasks goes
  tcp-dump                network capture: resets, TLS alerts, Kafka errors
  jscissors               traced method calls: arguments, durations, exceptions

playground connector oracle-cdc-xstream generate-report,
playground debug cfk generate-bundle.

🔬 Analyze a heap dump with Eclipse Memory Analyzer (MAT), run headless in Docker

subcommands.name: logs
subcommands.description:
🔥 Show a digest of ERROR/FATAL records found in log files, folders or zip bundles

The offline counterpart of 'playground container logs --errors', for
logs that do not come from a running container: a customer support
bundle, a CI artifact, a log file you were sent.

Repeated records are de-duplicated with an occurrence count, stack
traces are collapsed to the exception chain ("Caused by:") plus a few
frames of the deepest cause. Only records with an explicit level are
reported (" ERROR ", "[ERROR]", level=error, "level":"error"), plus
uncaught java exceptions: records logged at INFO/DEBUG/TRACE, and
level-less lines that merely contain "error" or "failed", never are.

📂 Folders are scanned recursively. .zip, .tar, .tar.gz and .tgz files
are extracted in a temporary folder, .gz files are decompressed on the
fly, binary files are skipped, and so are the copies of a file or of a
CFK support bundle already analyzed (an archive next to its extracted
folder). Only files with findings are shown. The HTML report also has
the configuration: the configs logged at startup (KafkaConfig values:,
DistributedConfig, connector and client configs…) and the .properties
and connector JSON files of the input.

☸️ A Confluent for Kubernetes (CFK) support bundle (kubectl confluent support-bundle or playground debug cfk generate-bundle: a folder with cluster-details.txt, or with cluster-resources/ and operator/; or a flat collection of kubectl outputs with a confluent-operator-*.log or the YAML of a platform.confluent.io custom resource at its top), alone or inside a folder or an archive, is detected and analyzed as a whole, in a Docker image built on first use: Warning events, pods (phase, waiting reasons, restarts, OOMKilled), every platform.confluent.io custom resource (phase/state, ready replicas, False conditions, failed connector tasks), the environment checked against the CFK support matrix (Kubernetes, CFK operator, CP and init container versions), the recent changes (who edited which CR and when, StatefulSet rollouts, pod restarts), the configuration (kafka.properties, zookeeper.properties, schemaregistry.properties, connect.properties and controlcenter.properties rendered by CFK, configOverrides, config logged at startup, connector configs from the Connector CRs and the config dumps of the logs), a JVM default truststore set without its password, and the ERROR/FATAL records of its logs, sorted into ~30 categories (pod failures, TLS, auth, MDS/RBAC, license, KRaft, replication, storage, scheduling…) with remediation steps. 📕 The log messages and events of known CFK problems (CFK triage table of Confluent support: roll blocked by the pre-roll checks, expired certificate, INCONSISTENT_CLUSTER_ID, ZooKeeper to KRaft migration, authorizer timeout, license secret…) are listed first, with what they mean and the KB / docs to read; PLAYGROUND_CFK_RUNBOOKS_FILE adds the internal runbook links of Confluent support (🔒 in the terminal, the HTML report and --json). 🔄 A CR whose image is not what its StatefulSet or pods run (operator did not apply it, roll not complete) is one finding, the exceeded quota events become one finding per ResourceQuota, each Warning event is counted once (event.txt and event.yaml) and a copy of the bundle inside the bundle is analyzed once. 🕰️ The time range of each log is listed, with a finding when a log starts long after its pod or after the last change of the CRs, and CRs that keep the "Reconcile is blocked" condition after the annotation was removed are one finding. 🕒 The changes of the CRs in the hour before the first critical / high issue are marked and listed in one finding. 🧩 A Connect whose spec.build.onDemand plugins cannot be installed (config-init-container failing, install error, slow init) and a Connector CR whose class is not installed are findings with next steps. 🔁 With several CFK bundles (-f a.tgz -f b.tgz), they are compared, sorted by collection time: same cluster or not, versions, changes of the CRs between them, issues fixed / new / still there, known CFK issues, with a verdict (HTML report, "comparison" in --json). 🚚 A ZooKeeper to KRaft migration gets its own finding: phase / sub-phase of the KRaftMigrationJob, how long it has been there (events, operator requeues), its last error and the next steps of that sub-phase (DUAL-WRITE waiting for the finalize annotation is low). Probe failures and back-offs of a pod that is Running and Ready in the bundle are low and marked transient. Each issue is attributed to a component and an instance (CR name), and to its connector: --component keeps some of them, the HTML report has Component / Instance / Connector filters. 🔒 --sanitize replaces secrets, IPs, hostnames, emails and LDAP DNs by placeholders (best effort: review before sharing). --logs-only gives the plain log digest instead. 🎯 --problem "<component, symptom, since when>" matches the bundle against what the customer reports: the issues that explain it first, a verdict (explained, not explained, not covered by the logs), the changes before the date. 📥 A Data to request section says what to ask the customer for next, with why and the command: from the gaps of the bundle (logs that start too late, previous logs of restarted containers, no events, no operator log), from its findings (OOMKilled, Pending pods, TLS, failed connectors) and from the symptoms of --problem.

🔒 With --sanitize, passwords and other secrets (password=…, JAAS configs, tokens, keys, credentials in URLs), IPs, hostnames, emails and LDAP DNs are replaced by placeholders (<REDACTED>, <IP-1>, <HOST-1>…, the same in the digest, the report and the JSON). Off by default: use it before sharing the output outside Confluent, and review it anyway (best effort).

🧭 After the digest of each file, a short summary: time range, occurrences by connector, known causes with what to do, root causes no known cause explains, and the configuration logged at startup (connectors, components, clients) with the keys changed between restarts. --connector keeps one connector, --show-config prints a configuration.

🌐 Also writes a self-contained HTML report in --output-dir, opened in the browser in an interactive terminal: verdict, known causes (task killed, authentication, TLS, unknown magic byte, OutOfMemoryError...), occurrences over time, root causes (deepest exception of each record), files with findings, and every distinct record.

🍪 Deep dive: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/deep-dive-container-logs
🎬 Bite size session: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/sessions?id=%F0%9F%95%B5%EF%B8%8F-a-connector-failed-read-the-logs-live-or-from-a-customer-bundle

subcommands.name: degrade-traffic
subcommands.description:
🐌 Add latency, packet loss, corruption or a bandwidth limit using tc

Some issues only happen on a slow or unreliable network: request
timeouts, retries, rebalances, producer or consumer errors. This makes
the traffic from a container slow or lossy, to a destination (and
port) or to everything, and --action stop puts it back to normal
without restarting anything.

Several effects can be combined in one call, e.g. --latency 100ms
--loss 1%. A new --action start replaces what was applied before on
the container. --action status shows what is applied and the measured
round trip to the destination.

tc runs from the nicolaka/netshoot image in the network namespace of
the container (an ephemeral container of the pod with cfk): nothing is
installed in the container, so it works with any image.

❕ tc only shapes the packets a container sends: with --latency 100ms
the round trip to the destination grows by 100ms. A container restart
removes the degradation.

🍪 Deep dive: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/deep-dive-network-traffic
🎬 Bite size session: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/sessions?id=%F0%9F%90%8C-a-slow-or-broken-network-on-purpose

subcommands.name: jscissors
subcommands.description:
✂️ Trace the calls of any method of a running JVM: arguments, return values, durations, exceptions, call tree

A java agent (tools/jscissors/agent, byte-buddy) loaded in the JVM of the container instruments the methods matching --class and --method, and records every call with what the --operation flags ask for. For a window of any length: --action start, reproduce the problem, --action stop, which copies the trace to --output-dir and analyzes it with playground analyze jscissors (methods by total time, exceptions, calls still running, slowest calls, call trees, HTML report), unless --no-analyze. With --duration, start, wait and stop in one command.

💉 No restart: the agent is loaded in the running JVM with the attach protocol (what jcmd does, without jcmd, which the cp images do not have), or over JMX for a JDK older than 16. --action stop restores the original classes. Starting again replaces the rules. With --restart, the container is recreated with the agent in JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, to trace the startup of the JVM too (or when the JVM refuses the attach).

🎯 --class and --method are exact names, or java regular expressions as soon as they hold other characters than letters, digits, '.', '$' and '_' (io.confluent.connect.jdbc.*, .*[Ww]rite.*). Only concrete methods are traced (trace the implementation class, not the interface), constructors and JDK classes (java.*, javax.*) are not. A class loaded after the start is instrumented when it loads.

🛡️ Safe by default: values are cut to --max-value-length and the secrets found in them are masked (passwords of maps, JAAS, connection strings), at most --max-calls calls (--max-calls-per-method per method) are recorded with their details (every call is counted in the statistics), or only the ones that throw (--only-failed) or are slow (--slower-than), at most 10 thread dumps and 1 heap dump, the agent can never throw in the traced code, and a toString() of an argument is never traced. Trace what you need: a regex matching thousands of hot methods slows the JVM down.

📂 In the trace folder (jscissors-<container>-<date>/pid-<pid>/): events.jsonl (one event per call enter / exit / dump), summary.json (statistics), agent.log, instrumented.txt, dumps/, and the HTML report.

🔖 The session of each container is kept in playground.ini (jscissors.<container>), --action status shows it with the calls so far. The agent jar is built from tools/jscissors/agent with maven in a container the first time (and after a change of its sources).

🍪 Deep dive: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/deep-dive-jvm-diagnostics
🎬 Bite size session: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/sessions?id=%E2%9C%82%EF%B8%8F-records-vanish-a-task-hangs-what-does-the-code-do

subcommands.name: topic
subcommands.description:
🗳 Topic commands

Produce, consume and manage topics without dealing with the kafka-* shell
scripts: the bootstrap server, the security properties and the schema
registry url are all derived from the running environment, so the same
command works on plaintext, on sasl-ssl and on Confluent Cloud.

📤 Get data in
  produce         generate records from a schema, or from your own data
  create          create a topic with the partitions you need

📥 Get data out
  consume         read from the beginning, deserialising automatically
  get-number-records   count what is in the topic
  wait-for-records     wait until the topic contains N records
  get-offsets          earliest and latest offsets per partition
  display-consumer-offsets   read the internal offsets topic

🔧 Manage
  list / describe / alter / delete
  reassign / elect-leader   move replicas between brokers, move leaders
  dlq inspect / replay   dead letter queue grouped by error, and replay
  set-schema-compatibility   compatibility of the topic subjects
  tag             stream catalog tags (Confluent Cloud only)

Serialisation is handled for you: 'produce' registers the schema you give
it and 'consume' works out from the payload whether it is avro, protobuf,
json schema or plain text.

🎓 Tip: in an example script, 'consume --min-expected-messages N' is the
assertion that the data made it through; it fails the run if it did not.
