subcommands.name: reassign
subcommands.description:
🔀 Move the replicas of a topic to other brokers

Wraps kafka-reassign-partitions, to reproduce a partition
reassignment or a rebalance (needs several brokers: playground run
--enable-multiple-brokers, brokers 1, 2 and 3). Set one of:

  --replicas 2,3   the replicas of every partition (or of --partition):
                   the first one is the preferred leader
  --brokers 1,2,3  a balanced plan over these brokers, generated by
                   kafka-reassign-partitions --generate (same
                   replication factor)

Displays the current and the new assignment, executes it, and waits
until the reassignment is completed (kafka-reassign-partitions
--verify, which also removes the --throttle). The leaders only move to
the new preferred replicas after a leader election: see 'playground
topic elect-leader'.

🎓 Tip: --throttle limits the replication traffic of the move, to
keep a reassignment running for a while (under-replicated
partitions, clients refreshing their metadata).

subcommands.name: elect-leader
subcommands.description:
👑 Elect the leaders of a topic

Wraps kafka-leader-election. By default, a preferred leader
election: each partition gets back its first replica as leader (what
auto.leader.rebalance.enable does every 5 minutes).

With --leader, a controlled leadership move: the broker is first put
first in the replicas of the partitions (a reassignment without data
movement, it must already be a replica), then elected. Useful to
reproduce a leader change (NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER, metadata refresh)
without stopping a broker.

--unclean elects a replica that is not in sync when no in-sync
replica is available (data loss).

subcommands.name: consume
subcommands.description:
📥 Consume topic from beginning

Reads from the earliest offset and deserialises records on its own:
the subjects <topic>-key and <topic>-value of Schema Registry decide
between the avro, protobuf, json schema and plain console consumers
(use --key-subject / --value-subject for other subject names).

🎓 Tip: --min-expected-messages turns it into an assertion. It waits
up to --timeout for that many records, consumes them and fails if
fewer could be consumed (records that cannot be deserialized do not
count), which is how examples verify that data actually flowed.

The consumer stops when no record arrives for 10 seconds (30 seconds
on Confluent Cloud), so it never waits for records that cannot come
(transaction markers and compacted records use offsets).

subcommands.name: produce
subcommands.description:
📤 Produce to a topic

See video tutorial https://youtu.be/mbzHCewG_XE

Generates records for you rather than making you write them. Give it
a schema, in avro, json schema or protobuf, and it registers the
schema and produces --nb-messages records of realistic random data.
The topic is created if it does not exist.

Three ways to say what to send:

  a schema on stdin           generated data matching that schema
  --value <predefined>        one of the bundled schemas
  --forced-value '{...}'      your exact payload, %g being the index

🎓 Tip: pipe the schema with a quoted heredoc, << 'EOF', so that the
%g placeholders survive the shell.

🍪 Deep dive: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/deep-dive-topic-produce
🎬 Bite size session: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/sessions?id=%F0%9F%93%A8-produce-realistic-test-data

options.description:
🗝️ Key to use. If not set, no key is used.

🔥 You can either:

* Set your own schema (avro, json-schema, protobuf) within single quotes (see examples) 

* You can also generate json data using json or sql format using syntax from https://github.com/MaterializeInc/datagen

* You can also generate json data using syntax from https://github.com/vdesabou/avro-random-generator (same as datagen source connector)

format of the records (avro, protobuf, json schema, plain json).

🌐 Also writes a self-contained HTML report in --output-dir, opened in the browser in an interactive terminal (--no-open to skip): known causes, when the records arrived, the groups with their original offsets and a sample value, and the replay commands.

  - under-replicated partitions (kafka-topics --under-replicated-partitions)
  - partitions under min.insync.replicas (--under-min-isr-partitions):
    acks=all producers fail with NotEnoughReplicasException (a topic
    whose replication factor is below min.insync.replicas is only a ⚠️
    warning: it is a config problem, not a broker one)
  - unavailable partitions, without leader (--unavailable-partitions)
  - the KRaft quorum: leader, lag and last caught up time of each node
    (kafka-metadata-quorum describe --replication)

Exits with 1 when the cluster is not healthy. With --wait-healthy, waits
until it is (for example after 'playground broker start' or a
'container restart'), up to --max-wait seconds.

Works on plaintext, secured environments and cfk.

💱 Transaction commands

Inspect the transactions of the cluster and recover from hanging ones
(wraps kafka-transactions). Works on plaintext, secured environments and
cfk.

  describe             one transactional id: partitions, duration
  describe-producers   producers of a topic, open transactions
  find-hanging         transactions forgotten by their coordinator
  abort                abort a hanging transaction

An open transaction holds the last stable offset (LSO) of its partitions:
read_committed consumers (sink connectors of a topic written by an
exactly-once source, Kafka Streams with exactly_once_v2...) don't read
past it, and their lag never drains. It ends when it commits, aborts, or
after transaction.timeout.ms. A hanging transaction never ends: find it
with find-hanging and abort it.

🐿️ Flink commands

Run Flink SQL and manage the jobs of the Flink cluster started with
'playground run --enable-flink' (jobmanager REST API on port 18081).

  sql         run Flink SQL statements (stdin or --file) with the SQL client

subcommands.name: sql

🐿️ Run Flink SQL statements with the SQL client

one SQL client session (bin/sql-client.sh -f) in the sql-client
container, or in the jobmanager container when sql-client is stopped. So
CREATE TABLE and the INSERT INTO that uses it must be sent in the
same call.

Results are printed as tables (tableau result mode). An INSERT INTO
submits a job to the cluster and returns right away: its job id is
printed, follow it with 'playground flink list-jobs'.

The client stops at the first failing statement, and the command
then exits with code 1.

🎓 Tip: a SELECT on an unbounded table (Kafka, datagen) never ends in
streaming mode: add a LIMIT, or SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'batch'
on a bounded source. Otherwise the client is stopped after
--max-wait seconds.

subcommands.name: wait
subcommands.description:
⏳ Wait for connectors to reach a state

Polls the connector status every --interval seconds until the connector
and all its tasks are in --state (RUNNING by default), and fails after
--max-wait seconds, displaying the status with the stack trace.

RUNNING is only reached when the connector and its tasks are still
RUNNING one --interval later, since a task is RUNNING before it
processes its first record and can fail right after.

When waiting for RUNNING, it fails right away if the connector or one of
its tasks is FAILED, since a failed task does not recover on its own,
and runs 'playground connector diagnose' on it: status with the trace,
digest of the connect errors since the wait started, offsets, next
steps and HTML report, opened in the browser from an interactive
terminal ('playground config open-diagnose-report-on-failure false' to
only print its path, PG_SKIP_AUTO_DIAGNOSE=1 for the status only).
A connector RUNNING without any task for 30 seconds (Replicator without
matching topic yet, JDBC source without table) is accepted with a
warning. A Datagen task that failed with "Stopping connector: generated
the configured N number of messages" ("iterations" reached) is
completed, not FAILED, and counts as RUNNING.
For the same reason, --state FAILED is reached as soon as the connector
or one of its tasks is FAILED (the connector itself usually stays
RUNNING when only a task fails).

🎓 Tip: 'connector create-or-update' already waits for RUNNING. Use
it for another state, or after 'connector create-or-update --no-wait'.

🍪 Deep dive: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/deep-dive-connector-create-or-update
🎬 Bite size session: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/sessions?id=%F0%9F%94%8C-the-sink-fails-right-after-it-is-deployed

connector convert'). Without stdin, --connector validates the config

🅾️ Specific Oracle CDC Xstream commands

individual query outputs.

🐞 Execute various SQL commands to debug xstream components

container and prints the results, with a link to the Oracle
documentation of each view:

  redo logs           the files each capture process still needs
  outbound server     general state, current transaction, low position

subcommands.name: test
subcommands.description:
🧪 Apply the transform chain (SMT) of a connector to a record, step by step

Shows what each transform changes (topic, key, value, headers, schema field by field), the result of each predicate, a record dropped by a transform, and the transform that throws with its config and its error. No topic or connector is created: the chain runs in a small harness in the connect container, with the classpath and the plugin.path of the worker, so the transforms, predicates and converters are the same classes and versions as in the worker.

The transforms come from a running connector (--connector) or from a connector config on stdin (or --config @file). The record is a json (--record): schemaless, or {"schema": ..., "payload": ...} like the JsonConverter for a record with a schema. Or a real record of a topic (--from-topic, --offset), converted with the converters of the connector (avro, protobuf, json schema with schema registry).

--cp-version runs the same test with the built-in transforms of other CP versions (throwaway cp-server-connect containers), --smt-plugin installs a Confluent Hub plugin for the test only (the worker is not changed), --smt-jar adds a jar (custom SMT development).

An html report of the steps (the value after each step with the added, changed and removed fields highlighted, the schema diff, the predicates, the error with its stack trace, and with --cp-version a comparison of the versions) is written to /tmp/playground-smt-test, and opened in the browser in an interactive terminal.

🎓 Tip: the connector config can be a whole connector config: only transforms.*, predicates.* and the converters are used.

subcommands.name: offsets
subcommands.description:
💈 Handle source and sink connectors offsets

Where a connector is in its data: for a source, the position it keeps in
the system it reads from (a SCN, a binlog position, a file offset); for a
sink, the consumer group offsets of the topics it consumes.

  get                          show them
  alter                        edit them in your editor, then apply
  reset                        start over from the beginning
  get-offsets-request-status   did the last change go through

This uses the first-class offsets API (KIP-875), so it needs CP 7.5 for
get and CP 7.6 for alter and reset. On older CP the playground falls back
to kafka-consumer-groups, which only covers sink connectors.

The connector must not be running while its offsets change: alter and
reset stop it and resume it for you.

🎓 Tip: a sink that reprocesses everything and a source that re-snapshots
are usually offsets problems, not connector problems. Look here first.

🍪 Deep dive: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/deep-dive-offsets-and-lag

Run it before and after alter or reset to check what really moved.

See https://docs.confluent.io/cloud/current/connectors/offsets.html

🆕 Reset offsets for source and sink connectors

Wipes the recorded offsets so the connector starts over: a source
re-reads its origin from the beginning, a sink re-consumes its topics
from the earliest offset. The connector is stopped and resumed around

subcommands.name: benchmark
subcommands.description:
🏎️ Benchmark the throughput of a connector

Measures how many records per second a running self managed connector
processes, so that two runs can be compared: another --connector-tag,
another batch size, another number of tasks. Everything runs on one
docker host, so the numbers are relative: compare runs on the same
machine only.

🎓 Tip: playground run --benchmark runs it right after the example (also
a toggle in the playground run menu).

--mode drain (default) pauses the connector, loads a backlog of
--nb-records, resumes the connector and measures the time it takes to
process the backlog. This is the most reproducible number, since it does
not depend on how fast the load is generated.

--mode steady measures the throughput during --duration (after
--warmup), while --stream-load-command runs in the background. When the
connector simply keeps up with the load (consumer lag of a sink, records
generated by the load of a source), the summary says so: the result is
then the speed of the load, not of the connector.

⏱️ For a source connector, --mode steady also measures the end-to-end
latency of the records: kafka record timestamp - time of the change in
the source system (a field of the value). After the measure, the
benchmark reads the records written to the topics of the connector
during it (all of them up to 100000, a sample spread over the measure
otherwise), and the summary, the result json and the report give its
p50 / p95 / p99 / max (over time, distribution, slowest records), also
in the comparable runs and the --connector-tag comparisons. When the
connector simply keeps up with the load, this is the number to compare.
The field is --latency-field, or the one the load writes the time of
the change to (create_ts of the CUSTOMERS table, update_ts with --shape
update), or source.ts_ms of a CDC envelope (commit time in the
database), or wallTime / clusterTime of a MongoDB change event. It is
not measured in a drain, where the latency of a record is the time it
waited in the backlog.

The load comes from the example:

  - sink connectors: the 'playground topic produce' of the example
    script that feeds the connector is replayed with --nb-messages
    <n> (same schema, key and headers), so every sink example that
    produces its data works without anything else
  - source connectors: benchmark-load.bash next to the example
    script, called with --records <n> --mode preload|stream --shape
    bulk|small-txn|update (rows in the CUSTOMERS table for the
    postgres, mysql, oracle and sql server examples, documents for
    mongodb, messages for ibm mq, mqtt, activemq, sqs, kinesis,
    pub/sub and cloudwatch logs, files for spool dir, filepulse,
    filestream, sftp, ftps, hdfs 2 / 3 and the generalized s3, gcs and
    azure blob storage sources, see the README of the example). It is
    called with --check first, so that an unsupported
    combination fails before the connector is paused
  - or --load-command / --stream-load-command, which take precedence

BENCHMARK_LOAD_SCRIPT=<file> uses another load script than
benchmark-load.bash: a file name in the folder of the example (or an
absolute path), e.g. one per reproduction model named after its ticket
(BENCHMARK_LOAD_SCRIPT=benchmark-load-123456.bash). It takes the same
arguments, and --enable-sql-datagen uses it too.

Throughput is read from the connect JMX metrics of the tasks
(sink-record-read-total: records read from kafka, including the ones
filtered or sent to the dlq; source-record-write-total), sampled every
--interval. Results are written to --output-dir (samples csv, result
json and an html report with the charts, opened in the browser at the
end in an interactive terminal) and appended to the benchmark-history
file, and the summary compares them with the previous benchmark of the
same connector in the same example (or with --compare <result json>).

Each result records the setup it ran on (host cpu and memory, container
engine resources, connect image and whether it is emulated, jvm and
heap, number of workers and brokers, environment, connector config with
secrets masked): the report shows it, and the summary warns when the
previous run was on a different setup.

🛩️ The connect workers are recorded with Java Flight Recorder during
the measure (over JMX: the cp images have no jcmd, nothing is
restarted), and the report and the summary say where the time of the
task threads went: running, blocked on the system behind the
connector, in the Kafka client, locks, waits; the CPU by layer
(connector, converters, SMTs, Kafka client, libraries, logging), hot
methods, allocation, GC, exceptions, with findings and next steps.
With --connector-tag, the versions are compared the same way. The
recording costs a few % of throughput: --no-flight-recorder disables
it, and the summary warns when the previous run was not recorded the
same way. The .jfr files are kept in --output-dir (JDK Mission
Control, or playground analyze flight-recorder).

📊 When Grafana runs (example started with --enable-jmx-grafana,
or --enable-sql-datagen), the measure is annotated on the Kafka
Connect, connector (Debezium, Oracle CDC, XStream, MongoDB) and
Kafka cluster dashboards, and the summary and the report link to
them at the time of the run (each version is annotated with
--connector-tag). Grafana is not started by the benchmark: its
JMX exporter and containers use CPU, and the summary warns when
the previous run was not measured the same way.

☁️ Fully managed source connectors (ccloud/fm-*-source examples that
ship a benchmark-load.bash, the one of the equivalent self managed
example: same local database or broker, reached by the connector
through ngrok): the records are counted from the end offsets of the
topics of the connector every --interval (its kafka.topic or
topic.prefix, and the topics consumed by the example script,
--topic to choose them), since Confluent Cloud gives no JMX: no batch
time, running ratio, cpu, gc, flight recorder nor --connector-tag.
A drain starts measuring at the first records seen after the resume
(Confluent Cloud takes a few seconds to restart the tasks, and its
status lags behind them), so the records seen by that first sample
are not measured. The throughput includes the network between the
docker host and Confluent Cloud. Run the example and answer n when it asks to
delete the connector, then run the benchmark.

☁️ Fully managed sink connectors: the load is the replay of the
'playground topic produce' of the example, like for a self managed
sink, and the records are counted from the offsets committed by the
consumer group of the connector (connect-<lcc id>). Confluent Cloud
commits them about every minute, so the end of a drain is known
within one commit interval: a drain that sees less than 5 commits
is reported as a lower bound, and the summary gives the
--nb-records of a drain of 10 commits (within ~10%, usually 1M
records or more).

📈 After the measure of a fully managed connector, the benchmark
reads its per minute metrics in the Confluent Cloud Metrics API
(sent_records / received_records, exact counts published about 30s
into each minute): the steady throughput is the median of the full
minutes of the measure (a drain of 3 minutes or more has one), which
does not depend on when a sink commits its offsets, and the put batch
time, batch size and dlq records fill the rows that JMX gives for a
self managed connector. The Metrics API uses the Cloud API key
(CONFLUENT_CLOUD_API_KEY) and does not answer for a deleted connector.

⚠️ Not available with the cfk environment yet.

🍪 Deep dive: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/deep-dive-connector-benchmark
🎬 Bite size session: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/sessions?id=%F0%9F%93%88-is-version-y-slower-benchmark-two-versions

📥 Command that loads the backlog in drain mode, instead of benchmark-load.bash (or of the replayed produce of a sink)

It runs with bash -c, from the current directory, while the connector is paused. It must create the records and return: --nb-records is then the number of records the connector should process, unless the command prints a line BENCHMARK_RECORDS=<n>.

Examples:

  # sink: 1M records in the topic of the connector (use the schema of its records)
  --nb-records 1000000 --load-command "playground topic produce -t my-topic --nb-messages 1000000 --value @predefined-schemas/avro/customer.avsc"

  --load-command "./load-my-table.sh 500000"

🌊 Command that generates load continuously in steady mode, instead of benchmark-load.bash (or of the replayed produce of a sink)

It runs in the background with bash -c, from the current directory. At the end of the measure, the file named by the BENCHMARK_STOP_FILE environment variable is created: the command should stop at the end of its current batch when it exists. It is killed after 120s otherwise, and killing a producer in the middle of a batch can send a truncated record to the topic. If it prints BENCHMARK_BATCH=<records> <epoch seconds> after each batch, the summary tells when the connector only kept up with the load.

Example, batches of 10000 records in the topic of the connector until the end of the measure:

  --stream-load-command 'while [ ! -f "\$BENCHMARK_STOP_FILE" ]; do playground topic produce -t my-topic --nb-messages 10000 --value @predefined-schemas/avro/customer.avsc; echo "BENCHMARK_BATCH=10000 \$(date +%s)"; done'

A line BENCHMARK_LATENCY_FIELD=<field> tells which field of the records of a source holds the time of the change, for the end-to-end latency (see --latency-field).

The original version is restored at the end, and the summary and the report compare the versions.

Example: --connector-tag 10.8.4 --connector-tag 10.9.9

⚠️ A downgrade or a major version change can be incompatible with the offsets or the config of the connector: the benchmark stops at the first FAILED state.

Repeatable: ✓ Yes

Default value: 1

📂 Folder for the samples csv, the result json and the html report (default is /tmp/playground-benchmark)

Default value: /tmp/playground-benchmark

🙈 Do not append the result to the benchmark-history file

🧵 Run the benchmark-load.bash of the example in <sessions> parallel sessions (default is 1)

A drain splits --nb-records between them, steady mode gives each session batches of --nb-records. Concurrent transactions are what a busy database looks like to a CDC connector (interleaved transactions in the redo log or the WAL, several open transactions). Only with the benchmark-load.bash of the example, not with --load-command.

Default value: 1

🛩️ Do not record the connect workers with Java Flight Recorder during the measure (no "where the time goes" section in the report)

⏱️ Field of the records of a source connector that holds the time of the change in the source system, for the end-to-end latency measured in --mode steady (kafka record timestamp - this field)

A dotted path for a nested field (after.create_ts, source.ts_ms), matched case insensitively, through avro unions. Its value can be an epoch in s, ms, µs or ns, an ISO-8601 string, or a MongoDB date or timestamp.

Default: the field the load writes the time of the change to (BENCHMARK_LATENCY_FIELD printed by benchmark-load.bash: create_ts of the CUSTOMERS table, update_ts with --shape update), otherwise source.ts_ms of a CDC envelope (commit time in the database), wallTime or clusterTime of a MongoDB change event.

subcommands.description:
🧑‍🎨  Create or update connector

The command every example uses to deploy its connector. The json config
is read from stdin, usually as a heredoc, so it stays readable in the
script. If the connector already exists it is updated in place, which
makes the command safe to re-run while you iterate on a configuration.

The command then waits for the connector and all its tasks to be
RUNNING, displays the connector status, and fails with the error if
they are not, so a broken config stops the example immediately instead
of failing silently later. A FAILED connector or task is reported with
'playground connector diagnose' (trace, error digest, offsets, next
steps and HTML report, opened in the browser unless 'playground config
open-diagnose-report-on-failure false'). When the script that runs is a reproduction
model, a connector that is not RUNNING is only reported as a warning,
since a reproduction model often creates a failing connector on
purpose. Use --wait to fail there too, --no-wait to skip the wait.

Fully managed connectors are only waited for with --wait.

🎓 Tip: add --validate to have the config checked by the plugin before
it is deployed, which reports every invalid property at once.

An update shows the keys added, removed and changed compared to the
running config (secrets masked).

The config can also be given as the path of a file, and in the
formats customers send (detected, see 'playground connector
convert'): the REST API format ({"name": ..., "config": {...}}), a
dump of GET /connectors?expand=info, a CFK Connector or Strimzi
KafkaConnector custom resource, a terraform confluent_connector
resource, or a connect-standalone .properties file. When the file
holds several connectors, the one named --connector is used.

A config that comes from elsewhere (a file, or one of these formats)
is adapted to the playground (--no-adapt to keep it as is, --adapt
to adapt a plain json heredoc too): bootstrap servers and schema
registry urls whose hosts are not containers of the playground,
the credentials of that schema registry, a license, replication
factors above the number of brokers, and on plaintext the security of
the clients whose bootstrap servers were rewritten. Masked secrets,
config providers of the customer environment (${file:...}),
terraform references and the keys still pointing to external systems
are listed. The heredocs of the examples are never changed.

🍪 Deep dive: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/deep-dive-connector-create-or-update
🎬 Bite size session: https://kafka-docker-playground.io/#/sessions?id=%F0%9F%94%8C-the-sink-fails-right-after-it-is-deployed

👨‍💻 Open an EC2 instance using Visual Studio code

Opens a VS Code window on the instance over ssh, using Remote
Development. The editor, the terminal and the playground CLI all run
there, so it feels like working locally while the containers use the
remote machine's CPU and memory.

The security group is refreshed with your current ip on the way, so this
is also the command to run after your ip changed and ssh stopped working.

🔐 Only your current ip address will be allowed to connect.

subcommands.name: sync-repro-folder
subcommands.description:
↔️ Synchronize reproduction-models folder between local and ec2 instance

The reproduction models you write are the only thing on the instance
worth keeping, and deleting the instance destroys them. These two
commands copy that folder in one direction or the other with rsync.

  local-to-ec2   push what you wrote locally, before running it there
  ec2-to-local   pull back what you wrote there, before deleting it

'playground ec2 create' runs local-to-ec2 for you, and
'playground ec2 open --enable-sync-repro-folder' does it again each
time you open the instance.

⚠️ Get into the habit of running ec2-to-local before
'playground ec2 delete', nothing else brings those files back.

Note: rsync needs to be installed

subcommands.name: push-secrets
subcommands.description:
🔐 Send the secrets store to an ec2 instance

Writes ~/.playground-secrets.properties (mode 0600) on the instance, which
the playground .zshrc sources on login. This replaces the encrypted
secrets.tar.gpg committed in the repository.

The file is piped over ssh, so no clear text copy is ever written locally
and the values never appear in 'ps'.

The credentials that cannot be stored as name=value pairs are sent too,
when they exist at the root of the repository:

  aws_credentials_with_assuming_iam_role       -> ~/.aws/credentials-with-assuming-iam-role
  aws_credentials_aws_account_with_assume_role -> ~/.aws/credentials_aws_account_with_assume_role
  github_ssh_key_file                          -> ~/.ssh/id_rsa
